533 Deploying, Updating, and Securing an Application with Kubernetes
So far, our application is up and running—but Kubernetes doesn't yet know how to tell whether our Pods are truly
healthy or ready to receive traffic. If the API process hangs or if a container starts slowly, Kubernetes will simply
assume everything is fine.
In the next section, we'll fix that by defining liveness, readiness, and startup probes. These probes allow Kubernetes
to monitor the internal state of your application, restart containers when they become unhealthy, and delay traffic
routing until they're ready to serve requests.
Defining liveness, readiness, and startup probes
Kubernetes gives i d x _ a 4 0 9 a 3 8 e us powerful mechanisms to detect whether an application is healthy and ready to receive
requests. These mechanisms are called probes.
A probe is a small diagnostic check that the kubelet runs against a container to determine its state. The results are
reported back to Kubernetes, which then decides how to react. The three main types are listed next:
Liveness probe: Detects if a i d x _ 8 8 5 f a a c 8 container is still running properly. If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the
container.
Readiness probe: Detects i d x _ d f 1 8 2 b 5 4 if a container is ready to serve traffic. If it fails, Kubernetes temporarily
removes the Pod from the Service's endpoints.
Startup probe: Used i d x _ e 2 0 4 1 3 f 3 for containers that take a long time to initialize. It delays liveness and readiness
checks until the startup completes.
By defining these probes, we allow Kubernetes to react automatically when things go wrong—for example, when
the API process hangs, or when the application is still starting up and should not yet receive traffic.

How rolling updates work
When you i d x _ c 4 e d b 8 6 5 update a Deployment in Kubernetes—for example, by changing the container image tag—Kubernetes
does not replace all i d x _ f 7 8 f 6 3 1 a existing Pods at once.
Instead, it does the following:
Creates new Pods based on the updated specification.
Waits for them to become ready (using the readiness probe we defined earlier).
Gradually terminates the old Pods as new ones take over.
This rolling behavior ensures that there are always enough healthy Pods available to serve traffic during the
update.
Let's experience this with a hands-on example.
Hands-on rolling update
In this i d x _ 5 6 2 6 c 3 4 e hands-on example, we will i d x _ 6 9 0 2 d c 8 b use our TaskBoard application to demonstrate the rolling update mechanism of
Kubernetes.
Step 1 – Verifying current setup
Before updating, let's confirm i d x _ e 3 3 1 5 7 3 b that everything is running as expected:
$ kubectl get deploy api
$ kubectl get pods -l app=taskboard,tier=api
$ kubectl get svc api
All Pods should be in the READY 1/1 or READY 2/2 state, depending on your replica count.
Let's also hit the /health endpoint of one of them:

--image=busybox:1.36 \
-- wget -qO- http://api:8080/health

version, the /health endpoint will also report the application's version number.

Step 7 – Controlling the rollout speed
By default, Kubernetes i d x _ 5 2 5 4 5 2 5 f replaces Pods gradually, but you can fine-tune this behavior. For example, to make the

strategy:

maxUnavailable: 0

Always add at most one extra Pod beyond the desired replica count
These values can be adjusted to balance rollout speed against service stability.

This strategy is known as a blue-green (or sometimes red-green) deployment.
Unlike rolling updates, blue-green deployments are not implemented as a built-in Deployment strategy. Instead,
they are typically achieved by running two separate Deployments and switching the Service selector from the old
version to the new one.
The idea is simple:
Blue (or red) represents the current production version
Green represents the new version waiting to take over
Both are deployed simultaneously, but only one is receiving live traffic
When testing confirms the new version works, we switch the Service to point to the new Pods

Our i d x _ 0 2 a 8 0 9 8 b current API Deployment is running version 1.0.0. Let's label it so that we can differentiate between the two
environments:
$ kubectl label deployment/api color=blue --overwrite
$ kubectl get deploy -l color=blue
You'll see the following:

Key takeaways – Zero-downtime deployments
In this extended example, we used the TaskBoard API to demonstrate both rolling updates and blue-green
deployments. A rolling update provides a gradual, automated rollout and easy rollback. A blue-green deployment
gives full manual control—two environments running side by side, with instant cut-over and rollback through a
single Service selector change. Both strategies achieve the same goal: zero downtime, but they serve different
needs.
Rolling updates are ideal for continuous delivery; blue-green deployments are better when you want to test and
verify before switching production traffic.
At this point, our application can deploy, heal itself, and update without downtime—but it's not yet fully secure. In
the next section, we'll explore security best practices for Kubernetes applications. You'll learn how to use RBAC,
NetworkPolicies, Secrets, and workload identities to protect both your clusters and your data.
Security best practices
Security is i d x _ c 0 3 6 2 b 0 2 not a feature you add at the end. In Kubernetes, we express i d x _ f 9 3 5 7 a 5 0 security as configuration—the same way we
define Deployments and Services. In this section, we'll harden the TaskBoard application with small, focused
changes that make a big difference in real clusters.
We'll cover the following:
Running containers as a non-root user
Using a ServiceAccount with the least privileges (RBAC)
Enforcing Pod security at the namespace level
Isolating traffic with NetworkPolicy (default deny + precise allows)
Managing secrets safely and rolling changes

Summary
In this chapter, we took everything we've learned about Kubernetes and applied it to a complete, realistic
application—TaskBoard.
We started by deploying a multi-service stack consisting of a database, backend API, and web frontend. We then
introduced probes to give Kubernetes visibility into application health, and saw how the platform can self-heal
automatically when something fails.
Next, we performed zero-downtime deployments, first using rolling updates and then blue-green deployments,
ensuring that new versions of our application can be released safely without interrupting users.
Finally, we focused on security best practices, running containers as non-root, applying the principle of least
privilege through RBAC, enforcing Pod security, restricting network traffic with NetworkPolicies, and handling
Secrets more safely.
With these building blocks in place, we now have a Kubernetes environment that is not only functional but also
resilient, secure, and ready for real-world use.
So far, we've worked entirely with local clusters. In the next chapter, we'll move beyond local development and
learn how to run containerized applications in the cloud.

What is the difference between a rolling update and a blue-green deployment?
Which Kubernetes resource ensures that a specific number of Pods are always running for a given

Why should containers in Kubernetes run as non-root users?

Answers
Once you've worked through the questions, compare your responses with the answers that follow. Each
explanation expands slightly on the concept to clarify not just what is correct, but why—solidifying your grasp of
how Kubernetes maintains, updates, and secures containerized applications:
Readiness and liveness probes allow Kubernetes to monitor the health of your application containers. A
readiness probe determines if a container is ready to serve traffic; Pods failing this check are temporarily
removed from load balancing. A liveness probe detects if a container is still functioning properly; if it
fails, Kubernetes automatically restarts the container. These probes help ensure HA and self-healing
behavior without manual intervention.
A rolling update gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, ensuring the application stays available
throughout the update. A blue-green deployment runs two complete environments (old and new) in
parallel and switches traffic from one to the other in a single step.
The Deployment resource manages ReplicaSets, which in turn ensure that the desired number of Pod
replicas are running at all times. If a Pod fails, the Deployment automatically replaces it.
You can simulate a failure by killing one of the running Pods (for example, kubectl exec <pod> -- kill
1) and watch how the ReplicaSet immediately creates a new replacement Pod. Using kubectl get pods
-w, you'll see the terminated Pod disappear and a new one start within seconds, demonstrating
Kubernetes' self-healing mechanism.
Running as non-root limits the impact of a potential compromise. If an attacker gains access to the
container, they won't have administrative privileges on the node or cluster. It also aligns with Pod
Security Standards and is often required in enterprise clusters where Pod Security Admission is enforced.
A ServiceAccount defines an identity for processes running inside Pods. Through RBAC, you can assign
specific permissions to that identity—for example, allowing it to read ConfigMaps or Secrets. This
practice enforces the principle of least privilege, ensuring that each component can only access what it

chunks.heading: Chapter 16 562
chunks.content:
truly needs.
A NetworkPolicy defines which Pods can communicate with which other Pods or external destinations.
By default, Kubernetes networking is open; applying a " default deny " policy and then adding specific

Secrets mounted as files are read directly from memory-backed volumes and are less likely to appear in
logs, process listings, or crash dumps. They can also be rotated without restarting the Pod, which makes
them more secure and flexible compared to environment variables.
Kubernetes uses the Deployment's rolling update strategy parameters (maxSurge and maxUnavailable)
together with readiness probes. It waits until a new Pod is marked Ready before terminating an old one.
This ensures uninterrupted service availability during updates.
Kubernetes does not automatically restart Pods when a Secret or ConfigMap changes. To ensure that
updated values take effect, you typically trigger a restart with the following:

monitoring, backup, and compliance mechanisms.
Setting up and maintaining such a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on your own infrastructure is a significant
challenge. You must provision and patch the underlying virtual machines (VMs), configure i d x _ d c 7 f c 4 2 b networking, handle
security updates, set i d x _ 0 c 2 5 f a 4 6 up high availability (HA), and i d x _ b a 4 8 8 5 2 2 ensure business continuity (BC). This is where the cloud
comes into play.

(EKS), Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), that take i d x _ 8 e 1 2 0 2 1 c away most
of the operational burden. They allow you to focus on your workloads instead of the control plane, networking, and
infrastructure maintenance. With just a few commands, you can create a fully functional cluster, deploy your
applications, and scale them up or down as demand changes.

Kubernetes offerings. We will also discuss when and why to choose a hosted service instead of managing

Why choose a hosted Kubernetes service?
Running Kubernetes i d x _ d d 7 b 0 d 6 c yourself is an educational and empowering experience. In the previous chapters, we used
minikube, kind, and Docker Desktop to create and manage our own clusters locally. These setups help us
understand the core Kubernetes concepts and how all components work together. However, building and
maintaining a production-grade Kubernetes cluster in a real-world environment is a different story altogether.
Operating Kubernetes at scale involves a long list of complex and time-consuming tasks. You must provision and
configure VMs, set up and maintain the control plane, manage certificates, monitor the health of cluster
components, configure networking and load balancers, and apply security patches regularly. On top of that, you

must ensure that your cluster is resilient, scalable, and compliant with your company's governance standards. All
of this requires deep expertise, dedicated operations staff, and continuous attention.
To address these challenges, all major cloud providers, such as i d x _ 8 e 5 1 e 5 1 7 AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud
Platform (GCP), offer i d x _ 6 a 5 4 d 0 a c fully managed Kubernetes services. These services take care of most of the operational heavy
lifting by managing the control plane for you, providing integrated monitoring, security, and scaling features out of

the box. You retain full control over your workloads while offloading the undifferentiated infrastructure work to
the provider.
Some key advantages i d x _ 8 4 1 2 7 2 d 5 of using a managed Kubernetes service are as follows:
Simplified cluster management: The cloud provider provisions and maintains the Kubernetes control
plane, applies patches, and ensures HA and reliability.
Integrated security and identity management: Managed services integrate seamlessly with the
i d x _ b e 0 0 1 d b 1 provider's identity and access management (IAM) systems. For example, AWS EKS supports IAM Roles
for Service Accounts (IRSA), Azure i d x _ 6 0 7 a 4 1 7 f AKS integrates with Azure AD Workload Identity, and GKE supports
Workload Identity for fine-grained access control.
Elastic scalability: You can scale your clusters and workloads up or down on demand. Many providers
also offer autoscaling features for nodes and pods, ensuring efficient resource utilization.
HA by design: Managed control planes are distributed across multiple availability zones and regions to
guarantee fault tolerance (FT) and i d x _ 4 d 1 c b c 4 1 minimize downtime.
Integration with the broader cloud ecosystem: Each managed Kubernetes service connects naturally
with other cloud resources such as container registries, managed databases, secrets managers,
monitoring, and CI/CD tools.
Reduced operational overhead: Teams can focus on building and deploying applications rather than
managing infrastructure, patching clusters, or troubleshooting control-plane i d x _ 6 3 5 2 5 e c 4 issues.
In short, managed Kubernetes services provide the same open source Kubernetes experience but with enterprise-
grade reliability and scalability. They enable organizations to adopt Kubernetes more quickly, minimize
operational complexity, and accelerate their journey toward modern, cloud-native architectures.
Other notable managed Kubernetes providers
Beyond the big three cloud vendors, several other i d x _ 2 b 9 8 f b c c providers offer managed Kubernetes platforms that cater to
specialized needs or hybrid environments. Red Hat OpenShift provides an i d x _ 3 5 b 1 7 a 5 1 opinionated Kubernetes distribution
with integrated developer tools, CI/CD pipelines, and advanced security features. It can be deployed both on-
premises and in the cloud. VMware Tanzu Kubernetes Grid targets i d x _ 9 0 7 b b 9 e b organizations already invested in VMware
infrastructure and offers tight integration with i d x _ 7 b 6 a d e 0 3 vSphere and NSX. DigitalOcean Kubernetes (DOKS) and Linode
Kubernetes Engine (LKE) are i d x _ d 0 9 3 2 7 c f lightweight, developer-friendly i d x _ 7 1 c b 0 a 4 d offerings ideal for start-ups or smaller teams
looking for simplicity at a lower cost. Finally, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Container Engine for

Cost and responsibility
While managed Kubernetes i d x _ 4 9 4 4 d 6 5 2 services simplify operations, they do not eliminate all i d x _ d 0 1 2 9 f e 9 responsibilities. Cloud providers
typically manage the control plane, including the API server, scheduler, and etcd database, while users remain
responsible for their worker nodes, workloads, and application-level configurations. You are still accountable for
security within your cluster, such as implementing RBAC policies, managing secrets, defining network rules, and
keeping your application images free from vulnerabilities.
From a cost perspective, you pay for two things: the managed control plane (which is usually billed per hour or per
cluster) and the worker nodes, which are charged as regular VMs. Although running Kubernetes in the cloud may
appear more expensive at first glance, the operational savings and the improved reliability often outweigh the
infrastructure costs. For most organizations, the trade-off between cost and reduced maintenance effort is well
worth it.
In the following sections, we will explore how to deploy a simple containerized application to three of the most
popular managed Kubernetes services: EKS, AKS, and GKE.
Overview of the managed Kubernetes services covered
in this chapter
The next three sections will i d x _ 5 7 8 9 0 0 7 4 demonstrate how to deploy the same simple containerized application to three of the
most popular managed Kubernetes services: EKS, AKS, and GKE. Although all three offerings are based on the same
open source Kubernetes foundation, each provider has developed its own philosophy and tooling around it.
Amazon EKS emphasizes i d x _ f 7 4 e 5 7 e c integration with the AWS ecosystem, focusing on security and fine-grained identity
management through IAM. Azure AKS provides i d x _ e d 4 5 8 f 4 1 a deeply integrated experience with Azure Active Directory, ACR,
and other native Azure resources. Google GKE, on the other i d x _ 2 6 0 b 8 5 c 7 hand, remains the most mature Kubernetes
implementation, as Kubernetes itself originated at Google. It offers sophisticated automation features, such as
cluster auto-repair, auto-upgrades, and an optional fully managed mode called Autopilot.
In the following sections, we will briefly review each of these managed services, create a small cluster, and deploy a
simple multi-tier application to it. While the setup commands differ slightly, the Kubernetes i d x _ 2 9 5 f 1 9 3 3 manifests and
deployment principles remain the same, demonstrating the true portability and consistency of Kubernetes across
cloud environments.
Running a containerized application on Amazon EKS
Amazon EKS is AWS's managed Kubernetes offering. It provides a production-ready control plane that is fully
managed by AWS, allowing you to focus on your workloads rather than maintaining Kubernetes i d x _ 1 a d 5 8 5 2 f itself. EKS
